title: De quibusdam eximiis proprietatibus circa divisores potestatum occurrentibus

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E557 sorts the primes p = 2m+1 for a fixed non-square base a. If a^m ≡ 1 (mod p), p goes in class T; if a^m ≡ −1 (mod p), p goes in class Θ. In modern terms this is Euler's criterion: T is where the Legendre symbol (a/p) = +1, Θ is where (a/p) = −1. Euler records only the reduced residue classes of the form 4n+1 modulo 4a. The classes 4n−1 follow from the rule that p and −p mod 4a lie in the same class, which is Euler's form of quadratic reciprocity. On the previous page he combines two prime factors f, g of a by intersecting classes: T_f∩T_g ∪ Θ_f∩Θ_g gives T, and the mixed intersections give Θ. This is multiplicativity, (fg/p) = (f/p)(g/p). He also uses φ(N) to count the classes: half of the φ(4a)/2 classes of type 4n+1 go to each of T and Θ.

On this page he tabulates the classes for a = 6, 10, 14, 22, 26, 15, 21, with moduli 24, 40, 56, 88, 104, 60, 84.

§33 (Problem) treats general composite a:
- If a = f², every admissible class lies in T and Θ is empty. Reason: a^m = f^{2m} ≡ 1 (mod 2m+1) by Fermat's little theorem.
- If a = f²g, the classes are those for g, minus the classes not coprime to f.
- If a = fghk, he computes classes for fg and for hk and combines them by the same intersection rule.

§34 works the example a = 30 = 2·15 modulo 120.
- The classes for 15, extended to 120, are T = {1,17,49,53,61,77,109,113} and Θ = {13,29,37,41,73,89,97,101}.
- For the factor 2, T is the classes ≡ 1 (mod 8) and Θ the classes ≡ 5 (mod 8).
- The common T-terms are {1,17,49,113}; the common Θ-terms are {13,29,37,101}. Their union is the T for 30, as stated on the next page.
errors: All seven tables on this page check out when recomputed via Legendre symbols: a = 6, 10, 14, 22, 26, 15, 21 all give correct T/Θ splits. The §34 intersections for a = 30 are also correct.
The 2° Θ list is printed out of numerical order (17, 33, 21, 29); this is cosmetic.

Logical gap: the claim that classes mod 4a decide everything, and that T and Θ always split evenly, rests on quadratic reciprocity. Euler had not proved it; here it is used as an inductively supported rule.
§33 does not explicitly handle a with an odd number of distinct prime factors (e.g. fgh). The recursion is implicit; §34 handles a = 2·3·5 by first combining 3 and 5.
Next page, not this one: the summary table for a = 14 omits 53 from the 14^m + 1 row, although it appears correctly here in 3°.

ideas.what: Splitting primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4) into classes mod 4a according to whether a^((p−1)/2) ≡ ±1 (mod p).
ideas.modern_name: Euler's criterion; quadratic reciprocity in Euler's form (a quadratic character mod 4a)
ideas.where_published: E164 (Theoremata circa divisores numerorum in hac forma paa±qbb contentorum), E552 (Observationes circa divisionem quadratorum per numeros primos, Opusc. Anal. I, 1783)

ideas.what: Combining the classes of the factors f and g by intersection to get the classes for fg.
Square factors are irrelevant: a = f² gives Θ empty, and a = f²g behaves like g away from divisors of f.
The 4n+1 reduced classes split equally between T and Θ (counted via φ on the previous page).
ideas.modern_name: The kernel of a nontrivial quadratic character has index 2
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (φ via E271); group-theoretic formulation later

deep.surprise_reason: The page consists of correct, routine tables and a recursive rule for composite a, illustrating Euler's well-documented empirical form of quadratic reciprocity and the multiplicativity of the character. It is already known and credited.
transcription_corrections: In §33, 'pro ipso numero f perinde' reads in the print as 'f' but should logically be 'a' (the full composite number); this is likely a misprint in the original.
In 2°, the Θ list is correctly transcribed as printed (17, 33, 21, 29), out of numerical order.
§34: 'reperientur' at the bottom of the page should read 'reperiuntur', as in the image ('vtrique T reperiuntur').
